In this smaller range we construct an honest private confidence set whose diameter is of the private minimax order on each of the two classes. As in the non-private case, the threshold arises because an honest set cannot, at a smooth density, be narrower than the separation rate arising in a related testing problem. Under LDP we prove that this private testing rate is of order $(nα^2)^{-2r/(4r+3)}$, which is at most the private estimation rate $(nα^2)^{-s/(2s+2)}$ over the smooth class exactly when $s \le 4r/3$. For $s > 4r/3$, however, we show that smooth-rate adaptation becomes possible once one discards from the rough class the densities that lie outside the smooth class but within an $L^2$-radius of the order of the private testing rate.

title: Exact Privacy--Distortion Design of Support-Constrained Randomized Response
summary: Full-support local randomizers can incur unnecessary reporting distortion on ordered alphabets. We study randomized response whose output is restricted to a radius-$t$ neighborhood of the private input. Input-dependent supports create privacy leakage at their boundaries, so ordinary likelihood-ratio calibration is no longer sufficient. Under approximate local privacy restricted to input pairs at distance at most $H$, we derive the exact hockey-stick defect of the mechanism. We then solve the joint design of the truthful probability, off-truth probability, and support radius. The fixed-radius optimum is available in closed form, while the global optimum requires only a one-dimensional integer search. We characterize both the privacy floor and its inverse, namely the smallest defect attainable under a reporting-distortion budget. We further prove that stringent approximate privacy forces the support size to scale as $Ω(H/δ)$. Deterministic evaluations illustrate the resulting tradeoff.

title: Penetrating the Reality Wall: Long-Range and Through-Wall AR/VR Privacy Eavesdropping via Wireless Power Side Channel
summary:
Over the past decade, Metaverse technology (AR/VR) has seen widespread adoption in numerous areas, including gaming, social networking, and online collaboration. Although recent studies have exposed vulnerabilities in VR systems, they often apply methods (e.g., pre-installed malicious apps or scripts) from conventional mobile platforms directly, demonstrating impractical attacks that fail to investigate unique privacy leakages specific to VR platforms. In this paper, we present an orthogonal attempt to analyze the attack surface of the power side channel on AR/VR's network connection by capturing the through-wall wireless power in the network transmission medium (e.g., Wi-Fi signals) non-intrusively in a comparatively long distance (e.g., 5.0m-8.0m) and further reconstructing multi-level privacy-aware user behaviors.
  We propose MetaSpy to validate the feasibility and practicality of our disclosed wireless power-based traffic analysis attack. It first captures through-wall wireless power transmitted from the Wi-Fi router of an adjacent room, identifies the device type, then infers (i) user interactions such as browsing websites, running AR/VR apps, and performing various in-app activities, (ii) unseen VR-specific activities in VR games (e.g., Population: ONE), and (iii) avatar-based user re-identification and virtual keystroke inference corresponding to head movements. We evaluated the effectiveness of MetaSpy in four commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) VR headsets, and the empirical results demonstrate its competitive accuracy in unveiling multi-level user privacy within virtual scenes in through-wall settings at a longer distance (1.8x-80x) than most of the recent studies, and it shows resilience to a series of external interference and impact factors. In addition, we also propose and evaluate effective countermeasures to protect data confidentiality in AR/VR wireless transmission.

title: Residual-Information Generalization Bounds Under Selective Privacy: Extended Version
summary: Information-theoretic generalization bounds usually control dependence on the task sample, whereas selective privacy may constrain only a different, private coordinate. We study i.i.d. pairs $(X,Y)$, where a learner observes $(X^n,Y^n)$, leaks at most $ε_n$ nats about $X^n$, and incurs loss on $Y$. A chain-rule transfer converts this mismatched constraint into the closed-form universal certificate $I(W;Y^n)\leq\min\{nH(Y),nH(Y\mid X)+ε_n\}$. Combining the certificate with mutual-information generalization yields a bound governed by residual task uncertainty and normalized privacy leakage. We derive complementary task-compression and individual-sample refinements, identify a sharp obstruction showing why selective privacy alone need not give a vanishing certificate, and invert the bound to obtain the exact leakage allowance for a prescribed generalization tolerance. We prove exact information-level achievability for deterministic-task and independent-residual source families and show that the resulting $\sqrt{ε_n/n}$ generalization rate is tight up to a universal constant. We also give a fixed-horizon adaptive application in which conditional leakage costs add.

title: Privacy Conductor: An Architectural Enforcement of Contextual Integrity in LLM-Based Document Retrieval
summary: Large language model (LLM) that retrieve internal documents within an organization must decide who may receive them. Existing approaches based on Contextual Integrity ask the model to make that decision, so access depends on probabilistic reasoning. We present Privacy Conductor, an architecture that removes the decision from the model: a deterministic gate enforces a policy written by an authority, and the model receives only what the requester may already see. On a synthetic clinical corpus of 2,520 requester--document flows, the gate reproduces its policy exactly, so the remaining risk lies in the document labels it reads. As label source is of primary importance, we compare LLM and human generated labels. Across seven configurations of six models from two model families, LLM-written labels degrade the policy in every case. Models assign a document's sensitivity tier correctly on 78--86% of documents, but reproduce its access-control list on as few as 23%. Relabeling the same documents five times with an identical request changes 13 to 124 access decisions per configuration, a result that does not depend on our own labels. On 214 flows from HIPAA court cases, the most accurate configuration (87.8%) still permits 11 of the 20 disclosures the law prohibits. LLMs can describe what a document contains, but not decide who should receive it. Hence, we recommend privacy policy should be authored by accountable personnel and enforced outside the model.

title: LiveAnon: Improving Privacy and Utility in Streaming Speaker Anonymization with Codec Language Models
summary: Speaker anonymization (SA) aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and emotion, but existing streaming systems often lose emotion information through discrete content bottlenecks or require emotion-specific modeling. We present LiveAnon, a voice-conversion-based streaming SA system that directly conditions an autoregressive codec language model on hidden features from a pretrained streaming ASR encoder, preserving emotion without emotion-specific supervision. To reduce codec-generation latency, we introduce capped RVQ decoding, which preserves dependencies among coarse codebooks while predicting the remaining codebooks in parallel. Under VPC24, LiveAnon improves intelligibility and emotion preservation over fixed-target Stream-Voice-Anon (SVA), a strong prior streaming SA system, matches emotion-prompted SVA in emotion preservation, and achieves the strongest semi-informed privacy among streaming systems. Under VPC26, it ranks second across all metrics among the evaluated anonymization systems, demonstrating a strong privacy-utility balance.

title: Towards Privacy-Preserving Thermal Human Perception from Dataset to Deployment
summary: Indoor human perception is the foundation for smart homes and healthcare. However, RGB cameras raise privacy concerns in private indoor environments, while low-resolution thermal cameras provide limited spatial and semantic information. Large-scale indoor thermal datasets and real-world deployments remain limited. Here, we introduce Indoor RGB-T, a large-scale paired RGB--thermal dataset for indoor human perception. The dataset covers 20 indoor rooms and contains 90,576 80x62 thermal frames, 87,016 temporally matched RGB--thermal pairs, and 115,557 annotated human bounding boxes. We establish benchmarks for robust thermal occupant-state detection with 0.75 mAP and occupancy estimation with an accuracy of 0.847 in unseen rooms. We further evaluate RGB-to-thermal and thermal-to-RGB translation, achieving a temperature MAE of 0.654 C and an R2 of 0.923. Finally, we deploy the thermal perception model on a commercial sleep-monitoring system in the real world. Field testing with 100 participants and deployment of approximately 1,000 devices further demonstrate its practical feasibility. We identify practical challenges that motivate future research directions, including environmental thermal interference, sensing range and multi-person occlusion. The code, trained models and partial dataset are available at https://github.com/kailaisun/RGBT and https://huggingface.co/skl24/RGBT.

title: AegisVox: Factorized Privacy and Clinical Preservation for Long-Form Speech
summary: Clinical speech reveals identity through both spoken identifiers and voice, yet its pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can also carry useful clinical evidence. Protecting that speech therefore requires more than preserving its words. We present AegisVox, a factorized framework that assigns consistent surrogate voices and edits identifier-bearing turns using document-consistent replacements. Across 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours, a matched comparison of two speech renderers separates replacement realization from retained identifiers, speaker linkage, and clinical preservation. Text-to-speech rendering realizes 535/601 planned replacements versus 453/601 for the codec-based speech editor. However, similar aggregate clinical preservation conceals more model-labeled contradictions, and conversation-wide speaker scores conceal greater edited-speech linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. Fresh transcription of original audio provides a reference for interpreting the clinical measurement chain; an independent judge tests sensitivity to model-based assessment. Better replacement realization can therefore coexist with worse clinical or speaker-linkage measurements. AegisVox supports use-specific evaluation of those tradeoffs, not a guarantee of identifier removal or clinical safety.

title: Minimax Wasserstein Testing under Differential Privacy
summary: We study Wasserstein-$p$ goodness-of-fit and two-sample testing under differential privacy. For general compact metric spaces, we establish upper and lower bounds on the minimax separation radii in terms of covering numbers, matching up to logarithmic factors. On the hypercube $[0,1]^d$, these bounds match up to constant factors for two-sample testing in all dimensions and for goodness-of-fit testing whenever $d\neq 4p$, thereby closing logarithmic gaps in existing non-private results. At the critical case $(d,p)=(4,1)$, we further show that a logarithmic factor is unavoidable by establishing matching minimax bounds for non-private Wasserstein-$1$ goodness-of-fit testing under a bounded-density assumption. Finally, for unbounded domains, we establish minimax-optimal separation rates up to logarithmic factors under an exponential tail condition.

title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
summary: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.
